narrative.morphology: Solitary planktonic trichomes, straight or slightly curved, several hundred µm long, 3-4 µm wide, with bluntly rounded or slightly tapered and often colorless end cells; scarcely constricted at the cross walls (Plates 1, 2). Vegetative cells are cylindrical, 1-3 times longer than wide, at the ends of the trichome, up to 6-7 times longer than wide, gradually becoming longer and often reaching 25-30 µm in length; with gas vesicles. Heterocytes solitary, intercalary (between two other cells; never at end of trichome), nearly spherical or ellipsoidal, 2-6 µm wide (median: 3.4 µm) and 2.5-9 µm long (median: 5.30. Akinetes (resting cells) oval, usually separated by vegetative cells from heterocytes on the same trichome, up to 3-14 µm (median: 6.7 µm) wide and 5-23 µm long (median: 10.2 µm), with a yellow or brown envelope. Reproduction by fragmentation of trichomes and by germination of akinetes. The species can be distinguished from the other common nostocalean cyanobacterium, Raphidiopsis (previously Cylindrospermopsis) raciborskii by its end cells. In U. ovalisporum they are thinner than the rest of the trichome cells and partly or completely hyaline with a blunt ending (Plate 2), as opposed to the pencil-/needle-shaped ending or a terminal heterocyte in U. raciborskii. Cell diameter is also larger in U. ovalisporum (Plate 3). Another, less common nostocalean cyanobacterium that should be distinguished from U. ovalisporum is Chrysosporum (previously Anabaena) bergii. (Stüken et al. 2009). The distinction is again by end cells (see item for Chrysosporum).
narrative.ecology: Umezakia ovalisporum, a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium, invaded Lake Kinneret in 1994 (Pollingher et al. 1998), shortly after the Hula Valley was hydrologically disconnected from Lake Kinneret when Lake Agmon was created (Hambright and Zohary 1998). This disconnection reduced substantially the nitrate load entering Lake Kinneret and created in-lake conditions suitable for the proliferation of nitrogen fixers. Umezakia ovalisporum was the first of several species of nostocalean cyanobacteria never recorded previously that appeared in Lake Kinneret since 1994 and got established in the lake. In September-October 1994 U. ovalisporum formed a massive bloom (Fig. 1). Since then, it is a common component of the Kinneret summer phytoplankton (Fig. 1). It occurs in the plankton only when the lake is stratified, peaking in September-October (Fig. 2). Cell diameter also fluctuates seasonally, having maximal diameter in winter, smallest in summer (Fig. 3). Towards the onset of winter, it forms akinetes (Plate 1) that sink to the sediment and wait for germination till the following summer. This species is usually evenly distributed throughout the epilimnion. In Kinneret it doesn’t form surface films or bundles.
narrative.environmental_conditions: Umezakia ovalisporum is adapted to higher ambient water temperatures, indifferent to the ambient Cl- concentrations, tolerates pH levels up to 9.2, beyond which it disappears (Fig. 4) and adapted to lower TP levels (not shown). In lab experiments, A. ovalisporum hardly grew under Na+ lower than 2.5 mM (Bar Yosef thesis, P.9, based on Kaplan et al. 1984. FEBS letters 176:166-168).
